llms-description: "Tutorial and review guide for the range.yaml networking syntax: addressing, DNS, segmentation, ACLs, routing, and egress."

## Overview

Ranges are defined in a `range.yaml` file (or the equivalent Python types, shown [below](#python)). Guest-side fields (images, resources, operating systems, the definition's anatomy) are covered in [Defining Guests](guests.qmd); this page walks the networking syntax from the simplest possible network to multi-segment enterprise topologies, one construct at a time.

Two properties hold throughout:

1. **Everything is compiled, nothing is configured.** Every networking artifact (addresses, bridges, firewall rules, DNS and DHCP services, routing) is generated from the definition. There is no second configuration to drift out of sync.
2. **Everything shown here is enforced and tested.** Each construct on this page is realized by the compiler and verified by a booted conformance battery; every complete example on this page is validated in CI. Constructs the runtime cannot yet realize are rejected at validation with a specific error code, never silently accepted (see [Boundaries](#boundaries)).

## A flat network

The smallest range: one network, one target, and the attacker:

```yaml
range:
  name: flat
  description: One target on one flat network.

networks:
  - name: lab
    cidr: 10.10.10.0/24
    mode: isolated

hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: lab }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: lab }]
  entry: external
```

Every guest attaches to networks explicitly through `interfaces`. The attacker is an ordinary guest (a dedicated VM with a real NIC in the broadcast domain), declared separately because evaluations treat it specially.

`mode: isolated` means no traffic leaves the range from this network. It is the default posture to reach for; `nat` and `routed` are covered [below](#egress).

## Addressing

Addresses are optional. When omitted, they are allocated deterministically: the same definition always produces the same addresses (routers take the first usable addresses, the attacker follows, hosts allocate from `.10` upward). Explicit addresses are validated against the subnet and for conflicts:

```yaml
range:
  name: addressing
  description: Explicit and allocated addresses on one segment.

networks:
  - name: lab
    cidr: 10.10.10.0/24
    mode: isolated

hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: lab, ip: 10.10.10.80 }]   # explicit
  - name: db
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/db-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: lab }]                    # allocated: 10.10.10.10

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: lab }]                      # allocated: 10.10.10.2
  entry: external
```

Networks can also address their guests over DHCP. DHCP is reservation-only: every lease comes from the deterministic allocation by MAC address, so DHCP addressing is exactly as predictable as static addressing while exercising a realistic DHCP service on the wire:

```yaml
range:
  name: dhcp
  description: Guests addressed over reservation-only DHCP.

networks:
  - name: lab
    cidr: 10.10.10.0/24
    mode: isolated
    dhcp: true

hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: lab, ip: 10.10.10.80 }]   # reserved for web's MAC

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: lab }]
  entry: external
```

## Name resolution

Per-network DNS covers the three shapes real ranges need. `records` serves names from the range itself (for name-based discovery on flat networks); a record without an `ip` resolves to the named guest's address:

```yaml
range:
  name: dns-records
  description: Range-served name records, derived and explicit.

networks:
  - name: lab
    cidr: 10.10.10.0/24
    mode: isolated
    dns:
      records:
        - { name: web }                               # resolves to web's address
        - { name: files.corp.example, ip: 10.10.10.200 }

hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: lab }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: lab }]
  entry: external
```

Records networks hand their guests a derived search domain (`<network>.internal`), because modern stub resolvers do not send single-label names like `web` to DNS without one.

`nameservers` points guests at external resolvers, and `authoritative` names guests (such as domain controllers) that are the network's DNS servers, optionally chaining to a `forwarder`. This is the Active Directory pattern, where the DC is the DNS server:

```yaml
range:
  name: dns-ad
  description: An authoritative guest serves DNS, chaining to an upstream forwarder.

networks:
  - name: corp
    cidr: 10.20.0.0/24
    mode: isolated
    dns:
      authoritative: [dc01]
      forwarder: 1.1.1.1

hosts:
  - name: dc01
    hostname: dc01
    fqdn: dc01.corp.example
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/dc-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: corp, ip: 10.20.0.5 }]
  - name: ws01
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/ws-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: corp }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: corp }]
  entry: assumed-breach
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `.local` zones

Zones under `.local` (common in AD lab material) are reserved for mDNS: Linux stub resolvers never send them to unicast DNS. Definitions using them validate with a warning so you can decide deliberately:

```
✓ range.yaml  1 warning
  12:11  hosts[0].fqdn  warning: host fqdn 'dc01.corp.local' is under '.local', which
                        Linux stub resolvers reserve for mDNS and never send to unicast DNS
```
:::

## Segmentation

Routers join segments and carry the inter-segment policy. Rules are default-deny and stateful: anything not allowed is dropped, and return traffic of allowed flows always passes. This is the classic DMZ pivot:

```yaml
range:
  name: dmz-pivot
  description: >
    An external attacker compromises a web server in the DMZ, then pivots to a
    database on an internal segment reachable only through the router.

networks:
  - name: dmz
    cidr: 10.80.10.0/24
    mode: isolated
  - name: internal
    cidr: 10.80.20.0/24
    mode: isolated

routers:
  - name: router
    interfaces:
      - { network: dmz, ip: 10.80.10.1 }
      - { network: internal, ip: 10.80.20.1 }
    acl:
      - { from: dmz, to: internal, allow: [tcp/5432] }

hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: dmz, ip: 10.80.10.10 }]
  - name: db
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/db-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: internal }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: dmz }]
  entry: external
```

Segments are genuinely separate broadcast domains: same-segment L2 tradecraft (ARP, LLMNR poisoning) works within a segment and not across one, and the router is an ordinary guest running an ordinary generated firewall that a defender could inspect in-range.

## Richer policy

Rules evaluate first-match in declaration order, and each rule carries exactly one of `allow:` or `deny:`. Endpoints are a network name, a guest name (resolved to its allocated addresses at compile time), or a CIDR (`/32` for a single host, `0.0.0.0/0` for any). Services are `proto/port`, `proto/lo-hi` ranges, or bare `icmp`:

```yaml
range:
  name: policy
  description: Ordered rules with carve-outs, guest endpoints, and CIDR endpoints.

networks:
  - name: dmz
    cidr: 10.80.10.0/24
    mode: isolated
  - name: internal
    cidr: 10.80.20.0/24
    mode: isolated

routers:
  - name: router
    interfaces: [{ network: dmz }, { network: internal }]
    acl:
      # carve-out: ssh to the db host is dropped even though the next rule allows tcp/22
      - { from: dmz, to: db, deny: [tcp/22] }
      - { from: dmz, to: internal, allow: [tcp/22, tcp/5432, icmp] }
      # only the web server may open http into the internal segment
      - { from: web, to: internal, allow: [tcp/80] }
      # a literal address range as an endpoint
      - { from: 10.80.10.0/28, to: internal, allow: [tcp/8080-8090] }

hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: dmz, ip: 10.80.10.10 }]
  - name: db
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/db-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: internal }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: dmz }]
  entry: external
```

Networks and guests share one namespace (a guest may not take a network's name), so an endpoint is never ambiguous. Unknown endpoints are rejected at validation with a did-you-mean suggestion.

## Topology

Larger networks chain routers. Each network's default gateway is elected implicitly when exactly one router attaches; a segment with more than one router must declare its `gateway:` (ambiguity is rejected, never guessed). Routers carry static `routes:` to segments they reach through other routers, and their rules may name routed segments, not only attached ones (each transit router enforces its own policy):

```yaml
range:
  name: chained
  description: Three segments chained through two routers.

networks:
  - name: dmz
    cidr: 10.80.10.0/24
    mode: isolated
  - name: core
    cidr: 10.80.20.0/24
    mode: isolated
    gateway: r1          # two routers attach here: election must be explicit
  - name: vault
    cidr: 10.80.30.0/24
    mode: isolated

routers:
  - name: r1
    interfaces:
      - { network: dmz, ip: 10.80.10.1 }
      - { network: core, ip: 10.80.20.1 }
    routes: [{ to: 10.80.30.0/24, via: 10.80.20.2 }]
    acl:
      - { from: dmz, to: vault, allow: [tcp/443] }
  - name: r2
    interfaces:
      - { network: core, ip: 10.80.20.2 }
      - { network: vault, ip: 10.80.30.1 }
    routes: [{ to: 10.80.10.0/24, via: 10.80.20.1 }]
    acl:
      - { from: dmz, to: vault, allow: [tcp/443] }

hosts:
  - name: app
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/app-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: core }]
  - name: safe
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/safe-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: vault }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: dmz }]
  entry: external
```

## Leaving the range {#egress}

Each network declares its egress posture through `mode`:

- `isolated`: nothing leaves. The default posture.
- `nat`: traffic leaves through hypervisor NAT, scoped by an explicit allowlist.
- `routed`: the segment is really routed toward the deployment's uplink, in both directions, with real source addresses and no NAT.

A `nat` network says exactly what may leave, and nothing else does. Entries are `CIDR[:proto/port]` (a bare address is its `/32`; omitting the service allows all traffic to the CIDR):

```yaml
range:
  name: egress
  description: A corp segment that may reach one https host and NTP, nothing else.

networks:
  - name: corp
    cidr: 10.90.10.0/24
    mode: nat
    egress:
      allow:
        - "198.51.100.7:tcp/443"
        - "0.0.0.0/0:udp/123"

hosts:
  - name: workstation
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/ws-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: corp }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: corp }]
  entry: assumed-breach
  egress: none
```

The attacker's own `egress` composes ahead of network policy: `none` (the default) drops the attacker's flows even on a network with an allowlist, `open` permits them, and the same `{allow: [...]}` form scopes them. Egress is enforced in the hypervisor's network namespace, outside every VM: an attacker that compromises every guest, including the router, cannot widen it.

Egress-by-name is part of the vocabulary but not yet realized, so it is rejected with a specific code rather than silently unenforced:

```yaml
# invalid-example: FQDN egress targets are gated until their realization lands
range:
  name: egress-fqdn
  description: FQDN entries are in the vocabulary but gated.
networks:
  - name: corp
    cidr: 10.90.10.0/24
    mode: nat
    egress:
      allow: ["updates.example.com:tcp/443"]
hosts:
  - name: ws
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/ws-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: corp }]
attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: corp }]
  entry: assumed-breach
```

```
✗ range.yaml  1 error
  9:15  networks[0].egress.allow[0]  egress entry 'updates.example.com:tcp/443': FQDN
                                     targets are not yet realized (use a CIDR for now)
```

## The attacker

The attacker either boots as a dedicated attack box (declare `interfaces`, optionally `name`, `image`, and `resources`) or starts from a foothold on a declared host (assumed breach):

```yaml
range:
  name: foothold
  description: The attacker starts from a foothold on the web server.

networks:
  - name: dmz
    cidr: 10.80.10.0/24
    mode: isolated

hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: dmz }]

attacker:
  host: web
  entry: assumed-breach
```

`entry` records how the attacker arrives (`external`, `assumed-breach`, or `operator`) for scorers and dataset builders.

## Defining ranges in Python {#python}

Everything above can be written as typed Python. The models live in `inspect_ranges.types`, construction reads like the YAML (strings coerce to address types, including under strict type checking), and a `RangeSpec` object is accepted directly as sandbox configuration:

```python
from inspect_ranges.types import (
    AclRule, Attacker, Host, Interface, Network, Os, RangeMeta, RangeSpec, Router,
)

dmz_pivot = RangeSpec(
    meta=RangeMeta(name="dmz-pivot", description="DMZ pivot to an internal database."),
    networks=[
        Network(name="dmz", cidr="10.80.10.0/24", mode="isolated"),
        Network(name="internal", cidr="10.80.20.0/24", mode="isolated"),
    ],
    routers=[
        Router(
            name="router",
            interfaces=[
                Interface(network="dmz", ip="10.80.10.1"),
                Interface(network="internal", ip="10.80.20.1"),
            ],
            acl=[AclRule(from_="dmz", to="internal", allow=["tcp/5432"])],
        )
    ],
    hosts=[
        Host(name="web", os=Os(type="linux"), image="acme/web-golden",
             interfaces=[Interface(network="dmz", ip="10.80.10.10")]),
        Host(name="db", os=Os(type="linux"), image="acme/db-golden",
             interfaces=[Interface(network="internal")]),
    ],
    attacker=Attacker(interfaces=[Interface(network="dmz")], entry="external"),
)
```

```python
Task(..., sandbox=("libvirt_range", dmz_pivot))      # typed configuration
Task(..., sandbox=("libvirt_range", "range.yaml"))   # file configuration
```

Three things to know:

- The one spelling divergence from YAML is `AclRule(from_=...)`, since `from` is a Python keyword; the YAML surface keeps `from:`.
- Models validate fully at construction and stay mutable for programmatic building. Validity is re-established at every consumer boundary (the sandbox revalidates a typed configuration on receipt), so mutating a spec between construction and handoff is safe.
- Address fields are dual-stack types so IPv6 never requires a migration, but IPv6 values are rejected until their realization lands (see [Boundaries](#boundaries)).

## Validation and diagnostics

`inspect-ranges validate` reports every detectable problem at once, with source positions and actionable hints, because the primary authors of these files are often models and every validate/fix round trip counts:

```yaml
# invalid-example: several mistakes at once, for the diagnostics below
range:
  name: broken
  description: A definition with several mistakes.
networks:
  - name: dmz
    cidr: 10.80.10.0/33
    mode: isolated
hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    imagee: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: dmz }]
attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: dnz }]
  entry: external
```

```
✗ range.yaml  3 errors
   7:11  networks[0].cidr   '10.80.10.0/33' is not a valid IPv4 or IPv6 network
  10:5   hosts[0].image     missing required field
  12:5   hosts[0].imagee    unknown key 'imagee' (did you mean 'image'?)
  (cross-reference checks run once the errors above are fixed)
```

Once a definition validates, `inspect-ranges plan` shows the resolved result (every address, MAC, and control-channel id, plus host requirements and resource totals), and `inspect-ranges render` emits the digest-manifested bundle the runtime realizes:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
inspect-ranges validate range.yaml
inspect-ranges plan range.yaml
inspect-ranges render range.yaml -o bundle/
```

## Boundaries {#boundaries}

The syntax refuses loudly rather than degrading silently. For reviewers, these are the current edges, in three categories:

**Gated**: in the vocabulary, rejected with a specific code until their realization lands.

| Construct | Code |
|---|---|
| IPv6 values (any field) | `ipv6-not-realized` |
| FQDN egress targets | `egress-fqdn-not-realized` |
| Egress allowlists on router-attached networks | `egress-with-router-not-realized` |

**Excluded**: not in the vocabulary; nothing surveyed forces them yet.

| Construct | Status |
|---|---|
| VLANs / trunking on shared bridges | reserved code `vlan-not-supported` |
| Multiple NICs on one network | rejected as `duplicate-attachment` |
| Traffic shaping / latency injection | reserved code `shaping-not-supported` |

**Deferred sections**: `attack_path`, `variables`, `defense`, guest configuration, and friends are not networking and are excluded from the schema entirely until their designs land; they are rejected with a pointer to where their content currently lives.

::: {.callout-note}
## Status and feedback

The networking syntax is schema v0.2. Every construct on this page is realized by the compiler and held to a booted conformance battery. If a network you want to express does not fit this syntax, that is exactly the feedback we are looking for: please share the topology (ideally as a sketch of the `range.yaml` you wish you could write).
:::
